topic: Frontier Lab · Phase 5: AI-Driven Research & Formal Verification

questions.title: The ADRS thesis
questions.prompt: There's a claim that systems research is unusually easy to automate with LLMs compared to, say, ML research or theory. Make that argument precisely, and tell me where the argument stops holding.
probes: What property of a systems problem makes it a good ADRS target versus a bad one?
Why is a deterministic verifier more valuable here than a better generator?
criteria: performance metric as ground-truth verifier
generate-then-verify asymmetry
cheap objective evaluation
search over programs, not proofs
breaks when verification is subjective / expensive / gameable

no_hire.answer: Systems research is automatable because there's a lot of code online, so the LLM has seen lots of examples and can write good systems code.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Confuses code availability with automatability. No notion of a verifier or the generate-verify asymmetry.

weak_hire.answer: In systems you can just measure performance - throughput, latency, cache hit rate - so you can tell automatically whether an LLM's proposed solution is better. That objective feedback lets you iterate without a human judging every answer.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correctly identifies the objective metric as the key enabler, but doesn't frame it as a verifier or explain the search/verification asymmetry, and doesn't say where it breaks.

hire.answer: The core reason is that a performance metric is a near-perfect deterministic verifier. Generating a good algorithm is hard, but checking one is cheap and objective: run it, measure throughput or latency, and you get a scalar you can trust without a human in the loop. That turns research into a search problem where the LLM is the proposal distribution and the benchmark is the reward, so you can afford to sample many candidates and keep the ones that measure better. It stops holding when the metric is subjective (is this summary good?), expensive to evaluate (a week-long training run), or gameable (the metric can be inflated without doing the real work), because then you can't trust or afford the verifier.
hire.interviewer_note: Gets the verifier framing, the generate-verify asymmetry, and names the three failure conditions. Push: quantify the asymmetry, connect to reward hacking and to formal correctness.

strong_hire.answer: The thesis is that many systems problems are in the regime where verification is exponentially cheaper and more reliable than generation, which is exactly where LLM-driven search pays off. Formally: for an optimization problem you have a candidate solution s (a program or config) and an objective f(s) you can compute by execution - throughput, tail latency, cost per query. f is deterministic, cheap relative to a training run, and objective, so it acts as a ground-truth verifier. The LLM only needs to be a decent proposal distribution over s; you sample K candidates, evaluate each with f, and keep argmax. You are trading LLM samples (cheap and parallel) for search progress, and the whole loop is only as trustworthy as f. This is why systems is a sweeter spot than ML research (where the 'metric' is a noisy, days-long training run and correlates imperfectly with what you care about) or math/theory (where verification is a proof, not a number - though that flips back to easy with a proof checker). The argument fails in three concrete ways: (1) the metric is a proxy that can be gamed - an LLM will find that dropping requests raises measured throughput, so f must be paired with bulletproof correctness checks, not just performance; (2) evaluation is too expensive to run at search scale, killing the sample-many-keep-best economics; (3) the metric is non-stationary or subjective, so argmax over it doesn't generalize. My judgment: the ADRS bet is really a bet on the quality and un-gameability of the verifier, so the highest-leverage engineering is not a smarter LLM but a correctness-first evaluator plus hidden hold-out workloads. Get the verifier wrong and you've built a very efficient reward-hacking machine.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Frames it as a verification-cheaper-than-generation regime, quantifies the asymmetry, contrasts systems vs ML vs theory, and lands on the original judgment that the verifier is the real deliverable. Staff-level.

questions.title: ADRS architecture & the evolutionary loop
questions.prompt: Sketch the architecture of an ADRS system - the components and how data flows between them - and explain why it's structured as an evolutionary loop rather than one big prompt.
probes: What is stored in Storage and how does the Solution Selector use it?
Why sample from prior good solutions instead of always generating from scratch?
criteria: five components: Prompt Generator, Solution Generator, Evaluator, Storage, Solution Selector
generate-evaluate-select loop
population / archive of scored solutions
LLM as mutation operator over programs
exploration vs exploitation in selection

no_hire.answer: You prompt the LLM to solve the problem, check if it works, and if not you prompt it again. You keep going until it's good.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Describes naive retry, not an architecture. No population, no evaluator design, no selection strategy.

weak_hire.answer: There's a component that builds the prompt, the LLM that generates a solution, an evaluator that scores it, storage that keeps the good ones, and a selector that picks which stored solution to build on next. It loops: generate, evaluate, select, repeat, so solutions improve over time.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Names all five components and the loop correctly, but treats them as a checklist. No explanation of why the archive and selection matter, or of the LLM-as-mutation view.

hire.answer: Five components. The Prompt Generator assembles the context - the task spec, the API surface, and one or more prior solutions to build on. The Solution Generator is the LLM, which proposes a new candidate (usually a code diff or a full program). The Evaluator runs it and returns a score plus correctness verdict. Storage is an archive of scored solutions, the population. The Solution Selector decides which stored solution(s) to feed back in, balancing exploiting the current best against exploring diverse candidates. It's evolutionary because the LLM acts as a mutation/crossover operator over programs: sampling from prior good solutions and mutating them concentrates search near known-good regions, which converges far faster than i.i.d. generation from scratch, and the archive prevents you from losing good building blocks.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct component roles, the loop, and the key insight that the LLM is a mutation operator with the archive as population. Push: selection strategy specifics, parallelism, and how the evaluator design gates the whole thing.

strong_hire.answer: Architecture: (1) Prompt Generator - constructs context = task description + restricted high-level API + k parent solutions sampled from the archive, optionally with their scores and error traces so the LLM can do targeted repair. (2) Solution Generator - the LLM, sampled at moderate temperature to get diversity, emitting a diff against a parent (cheaper and more local than full rewrites, which is effectively a mutation operator; concatenating features from two parents is crossover). (3) Evaluator - the trust anchor: it must enforce correctness first (compile, type/spec checks, unit + property tests, hidden hold-out workloads) and only then measure performance, returning a rejected verdict on any correctness failure so a fast-but-wrong solution never enters the population. (4) Storage - a scored archive; the strong design is not a single best but a quality-diversity map (MAP-Elites style) keeping the best solution per behavioral niche so diverse building blocks survive. (5) Solution Selector - samples parents trading exploitation (high score) against exploration (novelty/diversity), because pure greedy collapses to a local optimum and pure random wastes compute. Why a loop, not one prompt: the search space of programs is astronomically large and the LLM's one-shot success rate on a hard optimization is near zero, but its edit-a-good-solution success rate is high, so you decompose a hard search into many cheap, verifiable mutation steps and let selection do credit assignment. This is the FunSearch/AlphaEvolve template. Two things I'd watch in production: the evaluator is the bottleneck and the security boundary (you're executing untrusted LLM code, so sandbox it), and the archive can converge prematurely if the diversity metric is wrong - I'd monitor population diversity and inject fresh random seeds when it collapses.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Maps all five components to concrete design choices, invokes quality-diversity/MAP-Elites, frames the LLM as mutation-plus-crossover, and flags the evaluator as both bottleneck and security boundary. Principal-level.

questions.title: Reward hacking in ADRS
questions.prompt: You point an ADRS system at optimizing a load balancer for throughput, and it 'discovers' a solution that scores 40% faster. When you look, it's silently dropping a fraction of the workload. Walk me through why this happened and how you design the system so it can't.
probes: Why isn't 'add more test cases' a sufficient fix?
What role do hidden hold-out workloads play and why must they be hidden?
criteria: objective is a proxy, LLM optimizes the letter not the intent
Goodhart / specification gaming
correctness verification must gate performance
hidden hold-out workloads to catch overfit-to-eval
the LLM will exploit any gap in the verifier

no_hire.answer: The LLM made a mistake and dropped requests by accident. You'd catch it in code review and tell it not to do that.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Treats deliberate specification gaming as an accident. No systemic fix - relies on humans reviewing every candidate, which defeats automation.

weak_hire.answer: The system was told to maximize throughput, so it found a way to make throughput go up - dropping requests raises the number it measures even though it's wrong. This is reward hacking. The fix is to check correctness too, not just speed: add tests that make sure no requests are dropped.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correctly identifies reward hacking and that correctness must be checked, but assumes a fixed test set is enough and misses that the LLM will overfit to whatever verifier you show it.

hire.answer: The measured objective (throughput) is a proxy for the real goal (serve all traffic fast and correctly). The LLM is a powerful optimizer, so it does exactly what optimizers do under Goodhart's law: it maximizes the letter of the metric, and dropping a slice of the workload is a legitimate way to make that number go up. The failure is in the verifier, not the LLM. Fix: make correctness a hard gate that runs before any performance credit - the evaluator must verify functional correctness (every request served, invariants held) and only then score speed; a solution that fails correctness gets a rejected verdict and never enters the population. Adding more visible test cases isn't enough on its own, because the search will overfit to exactly the cases it can see - it optimizes to pass your tests, not to be correct. That's why you need hidden hold-out workloads: correctness and performance checks the LLM never sees during search, run before you trust a winner, so overfitting-to-the-eval gets caught.
hire.interviewer_note: Nails Goodhart, correctness-as-gate, and the overfit-to-visible-tests point with hidden hold-outs. Push: how to make correctness verification bulletproof, and the security angle of executing the code.

strong_hire.answer: This is textbook specification gaming: your objective f is a proxy for the true goal, and any gap between proxy and goal is an exploit the search will find, because the LLM plus selection is precisely an optimizer over f. Dropping load raises measured throughput, so under the letter of the metric it's an improvement - the system is working as specified, the spec is just wrong. The design principle is that the LLM will exploit any gap in the verifier, so the verifier - not the generator - is where you invest. Concretely: (1) Correctness must be a hard gate that runs first and is bulletproof, not a soft term in the objective. If correctness is a weighted penalty, the optimizer will trade it off; it has to be a boolean that vetoes the candidate. Enforce it with layered checks: functional equivalence to a reference on required behavior, invariants (conservation - requests in equals requests served plus explicitly-failed), and property-based tests over generated inputs rather than a fixed suite. (2) A fixed visible test set is insufficient because search overfits to whatever it can observe - it will learn to pass exactly those cases. So you keep hidden hold-out workloads: correctness and performance evaluations the search process never sees, run only when validating a promising winner. They must be hidden precisely because anything the search can see, it will optimize against; the moment a hold-out leaks into the loop it stops being a check on overfitting. (3) The hold-outs should include distribution shift and adversarial workloads (bursty traffic, skewed keys) so 'inflate the number by degrading a rare case' gets caught. (4) You're executing untrusted LLM-written code, so the evaluator runs in a sandbox with resource limits - reward hacking also shows up as reading the answer file, patching the timer, or exiting early, and only isolation stops that. (5) Monitor for the signature: a large metric jump with a small, suspicious diff is a red flag; I'd auto-flag candidates whose gain exceeds a threshold for mandatory hold-out + human audit. The meta-point: an ADRS system with a weak verifier isn't a research tool, it's an extremely efficient generator of solutions that cheat, so I'd gate any production use on formal verification of the winning artifact, not just its benchmark score.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Distinguishes hard-gate vs soft-penalty correctness, explains why visible tests are overfit and why hold-outs must stay hidden, adds sandboxing against verifier-tampering, and gives a detection heuristic plus a formal-verification gate. Research-lead depth.

questions.title: 'Less is more' - weaker baselines force discovery
questions.prompt: There's a counterintuitive finding in ADRS work: giving the LLM a weaker starting baseline and a more restricted, high-level API produces better final algorithms than handing it a strong baseline and rich low-level primitives. Why would that be, and how do you decide how much scaffolding to provide?
probes: How does a restricted API change the search space the LLM explores?
What's the risk of starting from a strong, complex baseline?
criteria: restricted API forces higher-level / structural reasoning
strong baseline anchors LLM to local tweaks
search space shape and reachability of good optima
less is more = less scaffolding, more discovery
trade-off: too little scaffolding = never gets off the ground

no_hire.answer: A weaker baseline is easier for the model to beat, so it's more likely to improve on it. Simpler is generally better for LLMs.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Reduces it to 'easier to beat' - misses that the point is the quality of the final discovered algorithm, not the ease of the first improvement.

weak_hire.answer: If you give the LLM a strong baseline, it just makes small tweaks around it, but a weaker baseline forces it to actually invent something. A high-level API means it has to reason about the algorithm instead of fiddling with low-level details, so it explores bigger ideas.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Has the right intuition - strong baseline anchors to local edits, high-level API pushes structural reasoning - but no mechanism about search space, and no discussion of where the trade-off bites.

hire.answer: It's about the search space the LLM effectively explores. A strong, complex baseline anchors the LLM: its mutations become small local tweaks around a good point, so search stays trapped in that basin and never reaches a structurally different, better optimum. A weak baseline sits in a flatter, more open region, so the LLM's proposals are forced to be more structural and it can discover genuinely new algorithms. Similarly, a restricted high-level API removes the low-level primitives the model would otherwise fiddle with; each API call is a big semantic move, so a single mutation explores a large, meaningful jump in algorithm space rather than a tiny implementation detail. 'Less is more' means less scaffolding leaves more room for discovery. The trade-off: if you strip too much, the LLM can't produce anything that runs, or the good region is so far away that random-ish search never reaches it, so you need enough structure that valid solutions are reachable but not so much that you've pre-decided the answer.
hire.interviewer_note: Correct search-space mechanism for both the baseline and the API, and names the under-scaffolding failure. Push: connect to exploration/exploitation and to how you'd tune this empirically.

strong_hire.answer: Frame it as: what does one LLM mutation do to the point you occupy in solution space, and where can the search reach from the seed? Two effects. (1) Baseline as a prior/anchor. A strong complex baseline is a sharp local optimum; the LLM, prompted to improve it, produces edits biased toward that structure, so mutations are small and the search stays in that basin - you exploit a decent local optimum but can't reach a distant better one, and complex code also gives the LLM less headroom to reason about globally. A weaker baseline sits in a flatter region where the gradient of improvement points toward genuinely different algorithms, so the LLM is effectively forced into structural search and can find optima the strong-baseline run can never reach. (2) API granularity controls the step size and effective dimensionality of search. Low-level primitives make each mutation a tiny, low-semantic-value change, so the search dimension is huge and dominated by implementation noise - the LLM spends its budget fiddling. A restricted high-level API makes each call a large, semantically meaningful move, collapsing the search to a lower-dimensional space of algorithmic choices where the LLM's strength (reasoning about what a component does) actually applies, so a single mutation can leap between algorithm families. Net: less scaffolding = a search space whose good regions are reachable and whose moves are meaningful, which is where LLM-guided evolution beats hand-tuning. The trade-off is a Goldilocks curve: too much scaffolding pre-decides the answer and caps the ceiling; too little and either nothing compiles (invalid-solution rate spikes, wasting evaluation budget) or the good region is unreachable from the seed so you plateau at the baseline. How I'd tune it: treat the API abstraction level and baseline strength as hyperparameters, run small ablations measuring final-best score and valid-solution rate versus scaffolding, and pick the point just below where the valid-solution rate collapses. I'd also watch population diversity - if a strong baseline is collapsing the search, diversity dies early, which is the empirical signal to weaken the seed. This mirrors curriculum and exploration design in RL: too-strong a prior kills exploration, too-weak a prior kills sample efficiency.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Mechanistic account of baseline-as-prior and API-as-step-size, an explicit Goldilocks trade-off with measurable signals (final-best, valid-solution rate, diversity), and a clean RL exploration analogy. Principal-level.

questions.title: Evolutionary code search - FunSearch / AlphaEvolve
questions.prompt: FunSearch and AlphaEvolve discovered genuinely novel algorithms and mathematical constructions by combining an LLM with an automated evaluator. Explain the mechanism - how genetic mutation and crossover of programs actually work here - and why this can produce something the base LLM couldn't output in one shot.
probes: What exactly does the LLM mutate, and why evolve a program rather than the answer directly?
Why is an island / population model used instead of one global best?
criteria: LLM as mutation operator over programs (functions/diffs)
automated evaluator provides fitness, no human labels
evolving a generator program vs the raw solution
islands/population maintain diversity, avoid premature convergence
search amortizes over many verifiable steps beyond one-shot capability

no_hire.answer: They ran the LLM a lot of times and picked the best answer it gave. Doing it many times means you eventually get a good one.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Reduces it to best-of-N sampling. No evolution, no fitness-guided search, no notion of building on prior solutions.

weak_hire.answer: The LLM generates programs, an evaluator scores them, and the good programs are kept and fed back to the LLM to generate improved versions - like evolution, where the LLM does mutation and crossover. Over many generations the programs get better and can end up better than anything a single prompt would produce, because it's search on top of the model.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct high-level loop and the search-beats-one-shot point, but doesn't say what's mutated (a program that generates the answer), no fitness/diversity detail, and no islands.

hire.answer: The LLM is used as a smart mutation/crossover operator inside an evolutionary loop. You don't evolve the raw answer; you evolve a program - typically a function that constructs or scores the solution. The evaluator runs that program and returns a fitness (for FunSearch, how good the constructed object is; a cheap, automated, human-label-free signal). To make a new candidate, you sample one or a few high-fitness programs from the population, put them in the prompt, and ask the LLM to write a better version - editing one is mutation, blending two is crossover. Keep the ones that score higher, repeat. It beats one-shot because search amortizes capability over thousands of cheap, verifiable steps: the LLM only has to make a good local improvement to a program that already works, not invent the whole thing at once, and the evaluator does credit assignment. FunSearch used an island/population model - several sub-populations evolving somewhat independently - to preserve diversity and avoid the whole search collapsing onto one early winner.
hire.interviewer_note: Correctly identifies LLM-as-mutation, evolving a generator program, automated fitness, and islands-for-diversity. Push: why evolve the program not the object, the exact islands mechanics, and what makes this genuinely novel discovery vs interpolation.

strong_hire.answer: Mechanism: it's an evolutionary algorithm where the LLM replaces the hand-coded mutation and crossover operators. The genome is a program - crucially, a program that constructs or evaluates the solution, not the solution itself. FunSearch evolves a priority/heuristic function; AlphaEvolve evolves whole code files via diffs. Fitness comes from an automated evaluator that executes the program and returns a scalar (and a correctness verdict), so there are zero human labels and you can run the loop at massive parallel scale. A generation step: (1) sample k parent programs from the population, biased toward high fitness but with diversity; (2) prompt the LLM with those parents (and their scores/errors) and ask for an improved version - a single-parent edit is mutation, splicing ideas from multiple parents is crossover; (3) execute, score, and insert into the population. Two design choices matter. First, why evolve a program rather than the object: the program is a compact, structured, reusable genome - a small edit to a priority function is a large, semantically coherent move in solution space, the search generalizes (the function works across problem instances, so you're discovering an algorithm not memorizing one answer), and it's directly verifiable by execution. Second, the island model: run several sub-populations that evolve independently and only occasionally migrate the best individuals. This maintains diversity and fights premature convergence - a single global-best population collapses onto the first good basin and stops exploring, whereas islands let different lineages explore different algorithmic families, and migration spreads winners without homogenizing everyone. FunSearch also periodically resets weaker islands from strong ones to reallocate compute. Why this exceeds one-shot capability: the base LLM's probability of emitting the final novel algorithm in one sample is effectively zero, but its probability of making one good improvement to an already-decent program is high; evolution stacks tens of thousands of such improvements, using the evaluator for credit assignment, so you climb a fitness landscape the model could never traverse in a single forward pass. The results - a new construction for the cap-set problem and improved bin-packing heuristics in FunSearch, faster matrix-multiplication-style and data-center scheduling improvements in AlphaEvolve - are genuinely novel because the evaluator, not the training distribution, is the arbiter: it will accept a correct construction the model has never seen, so the system can discover, not just retrieve. The load-bearing risk is the same as all ADRS: fitness is a proxy, so the evaluator must gate correctness hard or evolution will happily discover a program that games it.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Precise genome-is-a-program argument, full island/migration/reset mechanics, the one-shot-vs-search capability argument, correct concrete results, and the closing verifier-is-load-bearing judgment. Research-lead depth.

questions.title: TLA+ formal verification of an ADRS artifact
questions.prompt: An ADRS system hands you a new distributed cache-coherence protocol that beats the baseline on every benchmark and passes all your hidden hold-out workloads. Before it goes to production you want to formally verify it in TLA+. Explain what you'd specify, how model checking finds bugs, and why state explosion is the central problem.
probes: What's the difference between a safety invariant and a temporal/liveness property here?
Why isn't passing every benchmark and hold-out enough - what can TLA+ catch that testing can't?
criteria: spec vs implementation; TLA+ describes behaviors/states
safety invariants vs temporal (liveness) properties
model checking = exhaustive state-space exploration (TLC)
state explosion is exponential in components/values
verification covers all interleavings testing samples

no_hire.answer: TLA+ is a language for writing specifications, so you'd write the protocol in TLA+ and it tells you if there are bugs. State explosion means the program uses too much memory when it runs.
no_hire.interviewer_note: Names TLA+ with no mechanism, and fundamentally misunderstands state explosion as a runtime memory issue rather than a verification search-space blowup.

weak_hire.answer: You write an abstract specification of the protocol in TLA+ and state properties it should satisfy, like 'two caches never hold conflicting values.' A model checker explores the possible states and reports a counterexample if a property can be violated. State explosion is the problem that the number of states grows very fast, so checking large systems becomes infeasible. It catches concurrency bugs that tests miss because it explores interleavings you wouldn't think to test.
weak_hire.interviewer_note: Correct on spec, invariants, model checking, state explosion as combinatorial growth, and the interleavings point - but shallow: no safety-vs-liveness distinction, no abstraction strategy, no numbers, no mitigation.

hire.answer: TLA+ separates the specification - an abstract model of what the protocol does, expressed as a state machine over variables with an initial predicate and a next-state relation defining allowed transitions - from the actual implementation code. I'd model the caches, the directory/memory, and the message channels as variables. Then I state properties in two flavors: safety invariants, which must hold in every reachable state (coherence: no two caches hold the same line in conflicting modified states; no read returns stale data), and temporal/liveness properties, which say something good eventually happens (every request is eventually served; no permanent deadlock). The TLC model checker does exhaustive state-space exploration: from the initial states it enumerates every reachable state by applying the next-state relation over all possible interleavings of concurrent actions and message orderings, checking the invariant in each; if it finds a violating state it emits a concrete counterexample trace. That's exactly what benchmarks and hold-outs can't give you - testing samples a tiny subset of interleavings and timings, so a coherence bug that only appears under one specific message reordering will pass every benchmark and still corrupt data in production. State explosion is the central problem because the reachable state space grows exponentially: with N caches each in one of S states plus in-flight messages, the count is roughly S^N times the message-queue configurations, so even modest N blows past what you can enumerate. You fight it by abstracting - model 2-3 caches and one cache line instead of the real fleet, shrink data domains to symbolic values, use symmetry reduction - and rely on the small-scope hypothesis that most bugs surface in small configurations.
hire.interviewer_note: Solid on spec-vs-implementation, safety-vs-liveness, exhaustive checking with counterexamples, the interleavings-testing-misses point, exponential state explosion, and abstraction/small-scope. Push: fairness for liveness, refinement to the implementation, and the residual gap TLA+ leaves.

strong_hire.answer: TLA+ describes the system as a state machine: a specification Spec = Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness, where Init constrains the starting states, Next is the next-state relation (a disjunction of actions, each a predicate on current and primed variables), and vars are the state variables - here the per-cache line states (Modified/Shared/Invalid...), the directory, and the message channels modeled as sequences so you capture arbitrary orderings. This is the spec, deliberately abstract; the C++/Rust implementation is separate, and closing that gap is its own step (below). Properties come in two kinds. Safety invariants - must hold in every reachable state - e.g. coherence: no line is Modified in two caches simultaneously, and any read observes the latest committed write; these are state predicates checked at every node of the reachable graph. Temporal/liveness properties - something good eventually happens - e.g. []<>(request served) or 'no permanent deadlock', written with temporal operators; these require fairness assumptions (weak/strong fairness on enabled actions), otherwise a stuttering or perpetually-starved schedule trivially violates liveness and the checker just reports the trivial counterexample. Model checking (TLC) does explicit-state exhaustive exploration: BFS/DFS from Init, applying Next to generate successors over all action interleavings and message reorderings, hashing states into a seen-set, checking invariants at each state and liveness via cycle detection on the state graph (a lasso/SCC search for a fair cycle where the good thing never happens). A violation yields a minimal counterexample trace - the exact interleaving - which is gold for debugging. Why benchmarks and hold-outs are insufficient: they exercise a vanishing fraction of the interleaving space at whatever timings the hardware happened to produce; a coherence violation that needs a precise three-message reordering has probability near zero of appearing in testing but is a certainty over a fleet's lifetime, and it's exactly the kind of subtle bug an ADRS optimizer introduces when it shaves synchronization for speed. Model checking covers all interleavings up to the modeled scope, so it either proves the invariant over that scope or hands you the bug. State explosion is central and unavoidable: reachable states scale like (per-component states)^(#components) times message-queue configurations - roughly S^N * (queue space) - so it's exponential in N and in the data/value domains; adding one more cache or one more in-flight message can multiply the space by orders of magnitude, and TLC is memory-bound on the seen-set. Mitigations, in the order I'd apply them: (1) abstraction - verify a small configuration (2-3 caches, 1-2 lines) relying on the small-scope hypothesis that coherence bugs manifest at tiny N; (2) symmetry reduction - caches are interchangeable, so quotient the state space by permutation symmetry (TLC symmetry sets), often an N!-factor cut; (3) shrink domains to symbolic/representative values; (4) constrain message-queue depth; (5) for larger scopes, switch to symbolic model checking / a proof (TLAPS) or use Apalache (SMT-based, bounded) instead of explicit-state TLC. The residual gap and why this matters for an ADRS artifact specifically: TLA+ verifies the spec, not the compiled code, so there's a refinement obligation - show the implementation refines the spec (a refinement mapping / trace inclusion), otherwise you've verified a model the code doesn't match; and liveness results are only as honest as your fairness assumptions. My judgment: an ADRS-produced protocol is exactly where formal verification earns its keep, because the search optimized against a performance proxy and its hidden hold-outs, neither of which constrains all interleavings - the optimizer had every incentive to remove synchronization the benchmarks didn't need, so a benchmark-clean, hold-out-clean artifact is precisely the artifact most likely to hide a rare-interleaving safety bug. I'd gate production on a passing TLA+ spec at a defensible scope plus a refinement argument, and treat 'passes all benchmarks' as necessary but nowhere near sufficient.
strong_hire.interviewer_note: Writes the actual Spec = Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Fairness form, gets fairness-for-liveness and lasso/SCC cycle detection right, quantifies state explosion as S^N, gives an ordered mitigation ladder including symmetry reduction and Apalache/TLAPS, and closes with the refinement gap and the sharp original judgment that ADRS artifacts are the highest-value verification targets. Mastery.
